summary:
Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau ruled on 23 April 2024 that sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act, which criminalised consensual same-sex activity, were unconstitutional. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica, and as a result consensual same-sex conduct between adults is no longer an offence under the statute.

The change came through constitutional litigation rather than an act of parliament: the High Court struck the sections down as unconstitutional, so decriminalisation rests on a judicial judgment rather than legislative repeal.

The provisions had been under challenge for years before the ruling. In July 2019 Daryl Phillip, founder of the Dominican LGBT organisation MiRiDom, announced at a news conference that a High Court challenge to the buggery and sexual-activity provisions had been filed.

Human Rights Watch reported the decision on 24 April 2024 and called on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, placing the ruling against a regional pattern in which such statutes remain in force. Activists described the judgment as a significant milestone in the ongoing struggle for LGBT rights in the Caribbean.
tangentialFactors:
Dominica signed the joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity tabled at the Human Rights Council in 2011, one of 85 countries on the signatory list. That diplomatic commitment predates the 2024 judgment by thirteen years and is the clearest dated statement of the government's position on record in this inventory.

Local religious authority has also moved against criminalisation. In May 2013 Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica publicly called for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for an end to all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position.

Human Rights Watch's call for other Caribbean states to repeal comparable laws indicates that Dominica's decriminalisation is not regional: neighbouring jurisdictions retain sodomy statutes, so conduct lawful in Dominica may remain criminal elsewhere in the subregion.
localsOnly:
The litigation campaign was run by Dominican activists. Daryl Phillip, founder of MiRiDom, announced the filing of the High Court challenge in July 2019, five years before the sections were struck down, and the 2024 case itself was brought by a gay man living in Dominica rather than by an external party.

The Catholic Church in Dominica has a documented public position against criminalisation: Bishop Gabriel Malzaire's May 2013 call covered both the repeal of criminal penalties and protection from violence for LGBT people, framed on the Holy See's teaching.

Decriminalisation was achieved through the domestic courts, so the protection available to residents rests on a constitutional judgment of the High Court of Justice rather than on a statutory amendment that parliament could readily reverse.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition in Dominica, including change of name or gender marker on birth certificates, national identity documents or passports. That question is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening treatment of trans travellers is not sourced. Whether any documentary or medical screening at entry could disclose a traveller's gender history remains unresolved on this record.

The sources do not establish whether Dominican law provides hate-crime or anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, nor whether indecency, public-order or impersonation-type provisions continue to affect trans people after the 2024 judgment. Both points are unresolved.

Same-sex marriage and partner recognition, access to gender-affirming care, and rules governing restroom or other sex-segregated facilities are not covered by the available material and should be verified against primary Dominican sources before publication.
